title: Headlines from the New York Times
text:
Have you ever been curious about the hidden patterns behind New York Times headlines (…especifically Bill Clinton and Bosnia)? If so, you’re in for a treat! Using the RTextTools package, we’ll explore a dataset of over 3,000 headlines to show trends in the news of 1996 to 2006.
The dataset I am using comes from the RTextTools package and is documented
here. It is a dataset with labeled headlines from The New York Times, compiled by Professor Amber E. Boydstun at the University of California, Davis. As I stated previously, it contains information from 1996 to 2001.
It contains five variables — Article_ID, Date, Title, Subject, and Topic.Code.

library(tidyverse)
library(RTextTools)
data("NYTimes", package = "RTextTools")
nyt <- as_tibble(NYTimes)
head(nyt)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  Article_ID Date     Title                                   Subject Topic.Code
       <int> <fct>    <fct>                                   <fct>        <int>
1      41246 1-Jan-96 Nation's Smaller Jails Struggle To Cop… Jails …         12
2      41257 2-Jan-96 FEDERAL IMPASSE SADDLING STATES WITH I… Federa…         20
3      41268 3-Jan-96 Long, Costly Prelude Does Little To Al… Conten…         20
4      41279 4-Jan-96 Top Leader of the Bosnian Serbs Now Un… Bosnia…         19
5      41290 5-Jan-96 BATTLE OVER THE BUDGET: THE OVERVIEW; … Battle…          1
6      41302 7-Jan-96 South African Democracy Stumbles on Ol… politi…         19


Clinton was all over the news in the late 1990s. Here is a vizualisation of such:

nyt_clinton_week <- nyt |>
  mutate(
    title_lower = str_to_lower(Title),
    has_clinton = str_detect(title_lower, "\\bclinton\\b"),
    date = dmy(Date),
    week = lubridate::floor_date(date, "week")
  ) |>
  filter(has_clinton, !is.na(week)) |>
  group_by(week) |>
  summarise(n = n())

ggplot(nyt_clinton_week, aes(x = week, y = n)) +
  geom_line(color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "blue") +
  labs(
    title = "Fig 1: NYT headlines mentioning `Clinton`, grouped by week (1996-2006)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Number of Headlines"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8)








The story in figure 1 is clear! Clinton was seeking presidential re-election in 1996, then back in office in 1997 and then, from 1998 to 2000, the Lewinsky scandal and impeachment took place. In the 2000s, he was no longer in office, explaining the lack of mentions about him.
In 1997, Clinton visited Bosnia (did you know?). In that topic, how often is Bosnia mentioned in this time frame in the New York Times Headlines? Given Bosnia’s situation gained particular international attention in the very late 90s, let’s analyse the data in this dataset going till 1999.

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(RTextTools)

nyt_balkan <- as_tibble(NYTimes) |>
  mutate(
    title_lower   = str_to_lower(Title),
    subject_lower = str_to_lower(Subject),
    date  = dmy(Date),
    week  = floor_date(date, "week", week_start = 1),
    has_bosnia = str_detect(title_lower,
      "\\bbosnian?\\b|\\bbosnia-?herzegovina\\b|\\bsarajevo\\b|\\bbalkans?\\b"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(week))

count_bosnia_by_week <- nyt_balkan |>
  filter(has_bosnia) |>
  count(week, name = "n")

ggplot(count_bosnia_by_week, aes(x = week, y = n)) +
  geom_line(color = "black") +
  geom_point(color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Fig 2: NYT headlines mentioning Bosnia-related terms (weekly, 1996–1999)",
    x = "Week", y = "Number of Headlines"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)







lookaround <- nyt_balkan |>
  mutate(before_in = str_extract(title_lower, "(?<=\\bin\\s)\\w+")) |>
  filter(before_in == "bosnia") |>
  count(Subject)

ggplot(lookaround, aes(y = Subject, x = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Fig 3: Subjects appearing with 'in Bosnia'",
    subtitle = "1996-1999",
    x = "Subject", y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The mentions of Bosnia in the NYT headlines in figure 2 reflect its situation in the late 90s. This idea is further further complemented by figure 3. Mentions spike in early 1996 as post-Dayton peacekeeping and reconstruction in Bosnia dominated coverage, then fade through 1997–98. They surge again in 1999 when Balkans-wide news (especially the Kosovo conflict) drives headlines.

title: Room simulation
text:
Let’s imagine that dorm room assignments will be out soon, and you REALLY want to be paired with your friend. However, there is a catch: every assignment is completely random, so your seniority (or lack of therefore) or preferences are not taken into account at all. The simulation models this exact scenario: every student is randomly placed into one of the forty room slots, two per room, and we check whether student 1 (you) and student 2 (your friend) happen to share the same number. I am also assuming that in this specific college, there are no single rooms (or 3+ people rooms, by that logic!). Just double rooms.
I am running this simulation 1000 times to give us a more realistic sense of the chances of you being paired with your friend.
The function “same_room_once” randomly assigns 40 students to 20 double rooms and checks if you and your friend share a room. I chose map_lgl() in order to repeat the random assignment many times and estimate the probability empirically. The function returns TRUE if you and your friend end up in the same room, and FALSE otherwise.

library(tidyverse)

n_rooms <- 20
room_capacity <- 2
n_students <- 40

you <- 1
friend <- 2

same_room_once <- function(x) {
  assignments <- sample(rep(1:n_rooms, each = room_capacity))
  assignments[you] == assignments[friend]
}

set.seed(47) # I chose 47 as my seed because of Pomona College :) 
n_sims <- 10000

outcomes <- map_lgl(1:n_sims, same_room_once)
prob_same_room <- mean(outcomes)
prob_same_room

[1] 0.025


This code creates a tibble named “room_df” that lists our two possible outcomes, and subsequently assigns each corresponding probability(in “prob_same_room” and its complement “1-prob_same_room”). Then, to make the results more easy to interpretate, I use ggplot to graph the results.

room_df <- tibble(
  outcome = c("Same room", "Different rooms"),
  prob = c(prob_same_room, 1 - prob_same_room)
)

ggplot(room_df, aes(x = outcome, y = prob * 100)) +
  geom_col() + geom_text(
    aes(label = paste(round(prob * 100, 2), "%")),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 6
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "Probability You and Your Friend End Up in the Same Room",
    subtitle = "20 double rooms, 40 students, 10000 random assignments",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Probability (%)"
  )








As I previously mentioned, to estimate these probabilities, I wrote a function that randomly assigns 40 students to 20 rooms, each holding exactly two people, and then checks whether you and your friend share the same room number.The graph shows the probability of each of these events occuring.The insights of this code are a little sad: the chances that you and your friend will get paired up in the same double room are a mere ~2.5%. Therefore, you are way more likely to end up with someone other than your friend (~97.5%). The plot clearly illustrates this imbalance, with the “Different rooms” bar towering over the “Same room” one.

title: Dutch childcare benefits scandal
text:
For project 4 of Foundations of Data Science (R), I was tasked with exploring ethics and dynamics of power within data science, through a specific case study. The work is to be grounded on the following quotes from Data Feminism:

[Examine] how power operates in the world today. This consists of asking who questions about data science: Who does the work (and who is pushed out)? Who benefits (and who is neglected or harmed)? Whose priorities get turned into products (and whose are overlooked)? Source
How did we get to the point where data science is used almost exclusively in the service of profit (for a few), surveillance (of the minoritized), and efficiency (amidst scarcity)? Source.


The Dutch Childcare benefits scandal
What happened?
The kinderopvangtoeslag is a form of childcare support in the Netherlands. It is a government program that aims to help parents and caregivers in raising children. More precisely the program provides parents and caregivers an allowance to purchase licensed childcare from child care centers so that they can work during the day. Trying to prevent fraudulent claims, the Dutch Tax Authority implemented an automated risk-scoring system to identify “high-risk” applicants. The system quickly gained traction for its potential for discrimination, which was later proven to be true by the. The scandal took place in between roughly 2013 and 2019 (Hoogenboom, 2022). Amnesty International (2021) finds that the algorithm was found to disproportionately classify people with immigrant backgrounds, dual citizenship and women overall as fraudulent applicants to the program - with no evidence to justify the decision. Cases labeled as “high-risk” were often automatically assumed to be fraudulent, with little or no human review. Because of faulty data and an unchecked algorithm, thousands of people had to pay thousands in fines even though they were innocent, whilst also having their government benefits cut. Both Amnesty International (2021) and Hoogenboom (2022) find that the scandal played a significant role on why the Dutch government collapsed in 2021.
What is the permission structure for using the data? Was it followed?
Hoogenboom (2022) claims that individuals who applied to the program submitted their data on personal income, employment, nationality, and childcare provider in order to apply for the benefits. Its collection was considered legal on the grounds that it was to be exclusively used for determining eligibility and calculating benefit amounts. The Dutch Tax Authority however not only used this data to flag potential fraudulent applications, but did so with an automated risk-scoring system which used parameters such as immigration background and gender to score individuals with a lower/higher risk for fraud. Hoogenboom (2022) also shows that in 2020, the Dutch Data Protection Authority ruled that the Dutch Tax Authority illegally processed the sensitive data after multiple reports showed that the risk-scoring system the government body used showed biases towards minorities .
Who was measured? Are those individuals representative of the people to whom we’d like to generalize / apply the algorithm?
Hoogenboom (2022) claims that people measured in this situation were applicants to the program that primarily targeted low-income parents and caregivers and gave them the opportunity to put their child in daycare during the day so that they could work. In this light, the individuals are representative of the program’s target population.
Should race / nationality be used as a variable?
Although it could be argued that certain factors such as immigration background should be recorded in order to track the development of the program, here are a few reasons on why it should have not been used as a risk-assessment tool. Firstly, it purported to establish a causal link between immigration background and risk of fraud. Not only has this link been proven to be false in hundreds and thousands of studies, it is also important to acknowledge the history of these kinds of claims that helped eugenics movements rise in the 20th century. Amnesty International (2021) and Hoogenboom (2022) find that the scandal resulted in some of the most vulnerable families in society becoming even more marginalized. Thousands were forced to repay large amounts and lost access to essential childcare support. Many were pushed into poverty, eviction, and unmanageable debt, and there were widespread reports of severe stress, mental health struggles, and strained relationships, including divorces and family breakdowns. In essence, nationality and immigration background acted as a proxy for “likelihood of fraud”, enhancing systemic discrimination.
Is the data being used in unintended ways to the original study? The data was originally collected to support families with childcare costs (Hoogenboom, 2022) . It was phrased as a “tough on crime” approach that aimed to make the Dutch governmental system more efficient. Instead, it was used to punish and penalize the most marginalized and those whom the program was designed to protect. According to Amnesty International (2012)The resulting injustice sparked national outrage, parliamentary investigations, and ultimately contributed to the resignation of the Dutch government in 2021, and bringing to the surface the dangers of algorithms trained on non-representative datasets without meaningful human oversight.


Why does this matter? Who benefits? Who is neglected or harmed? Were the ethical violations in the interest of profit? Surveillance? Power?
The Dutch childcare benefits scandal is a clear example on the dangers of applying algorithmic risk-assessment systems in decision making without accountability or attention to power. It is hard to see who benefits from this situation, as even those who were not directly affected by the disaster, mainly the rest of the Dutch population, still suffered from the following government instability that ended in the fall of the government. In this way, everyone is harmed, but it is naive to claim that the harm was homogeneously distributed. Instead, as Amnesty International (2021) shows, the scandal resulted in hundreds of families going through unneeded stress and diverse forms of struggle, whose consequences can never be undone even with reparations. The ethical violations, which were covered with politicians’ “tough on crime” narrative, was a clear power and surveillance grab in a nation widely recognized for its democratic principles and norms, showing us that no government or state is immune from it, and how important transparency and oversight are in the deployment of algorithms in the public sphere.


Literature reviewed
Alexander Hoogenboom. (2022, November 2). Dutch Childcare Allowance Scandal: The importance of investigation powers. Equinet. (https://equineteurope.org/netherlands-institute-for-human-rights-role-in-the-investigation-of-the-childcare-allowance-scandal/)
Amnesty International. (2021, October 25). Dutch childcare benefit scandal an urgent wake-up call to ban racist algorithms. (https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2021/10/xenophobic-machines-dutch-child-benefit-scandal/)

title: Traffic stops
text:
For this project we will be working with data from the The Stanford Open Policing Project. The rich data collected by their team contains millions of traffic stops by law enforcement agencies across the United States. From this dataset, I want to see if there are patterns for what days of the week tend to have more vehicle traffic stops by law enforcement agents in the states of California, Oregon and Washington (west coast!),
First, we need to bring the data through SQL. This is important has this data set is so rich that importing it fully could crash our computers!

library(RMariaDB)
library(tidyverse)

With all of this information, we now need to join these 3 tables so we can do our west coast analysis.

ca_or_wa_weekday <- dbGetQuery(
  con_traffic,
  "
  SELECT
      'California' AS state,
      DAYOFWEEK(date) AS weekday,
      COUNT(*) AS total_stops
  FROM ca_statewide_2023_01_26
  WHERE type = 'vehicular'
  GROUP BY state, DAYOFWEEK(date)

  UNION ALL

  SELECT
      'Oregon' AS state,
      DAYOFWEEK(date) AS weekday,
      COUNT(*) AS total_stops
  FROM or_statewide_2020_04_01
  WHERE type = 'vehicular'
  GROUP BY state, DAYOFWEEK(date)

  UNION ALL

  SELECT
      'Washington' AS state,
      DAYOFWEEK(date) AS weekday,
      COUNT(*) AS total_stops
  FROM wa_statewide_2020_04_01
  WHERE type = 'vehicular'
  GROUP BY state, DAYOFWEEK(date)

  ORDER BY weekday, state;
  "
)
